AI-Assisted Coding vs Agentic Coding: A simple example¶

Jeremy Bloom 2026.02.03

I wrote this to provide a simple introductory example of both a) AI-Assisted Coding b) Agentic Coding, and how they are different. While real life examples are more complicated and typically combine multiple strategies, this should help illustrate the two fundamental approaches.

Let's say I want some python code that allows me to ask an LLM questions to get answers. To keep things simple, I have some basic requirements:

  1. I want to do this via an API in python
  2. I don't need the LLM to remember any state (i.e. what was the last question I asked)
  3. I want to be able to ask questions of different "personalities"

In Part 1 I will show building this code myself while asking questions of AI in a separate window. I can ask questions, copy code back and forth, etc. The key thing is I'm a very active participant in creating the code. This is broadly AI-assisted coding.

In Part 2 I will show building this code entirely through ab Agentic system. Here I just specify my requirements and then test the code.

Part 1: AI-Assisted Coding¶

1.1 Setup¶

To keep this example simple, I'll setup the build environment myself and use OpenAIs ChatGPT API interface to call the LLM. My environment uses uv which is common tool that replaces pyenv, pip, and more. If this is new to you, no worries, just keep in mind this does the magic of tracking and getting python and module versions so we can ignore it here.

If you want details, I (mostly!) did the following:

cd folder
uv venv --python 3.12
uv init
uv add openai
vi file.py

As a reminder, I'm using first Anthropic Claude and then OpenAI ChatGPT, separately, to update my code. My code uses openai, but it could just as easily use claude or the many other great LLMs, including Google's Gemini, Meta's LLaMA, Mistral AI, Cohere, xAI Grok, one of the many combined interfaces such as Amazon Bedrock or OpenRouter, a local LLM, etc.

1.2: Create and Run Starter Code¶

I start by creating some starter code. For those new to Python the first few lines may be confusing. Here's a quick summary, which you can safely skip.

  1. I import some pacakges, including openai to access LLMs, dotenv to access my LLM secret tokens, and IPython.display to help Jupyter display nicely
  2. I load my token into api_key
  3. I create the var openai_client_GLOBAL which, in this case, is a link to openai ChatGPT

Next I create my function ask_question(q, role_id) All it does is take a question and an optional role_id. While this is functional, it's kind of kludgy. There are a few things that aren't inline with best practices: 1) the roles are defined in the function, 2) the roles can't be seen outside the function, 3) caller can't identify a role by meaningful label, 4) it prints to screen rather than returning a string, and 5) it uses a global var. Not my best code, but here's the key part to remember: it's intent is clear. That's going to help our AI Assistant.

So I run the code can call it four times...

In [13]:
import os
from openai import OpenAI
from dotenv import load_dotenv
from IPython.display import Markdown, display

load_dotenv(override=True)
api_key = os.getenv('OPENAI_API_KEY')
openai_client_GLOBAL = OpenAI()

def ask_question(q, role_id = 0):
    ROLES = [
        "You are a helpful assistant",
        "You are a snarky assistant that gives misleading answers whenever possible",
        "You are a helpful assistant but talk in high and mighty language that many would find offputting",
        "You are a helpful assistant but speak like an ancient Roman senator - but still in english",
    ]

    messages = [

        {"role": "system", "content": ROLES[role_id]},
        {"role": "user", "content": q}
    ]

    response = openai_client_GLOBAL.chat.completions.create(model="gpt-4.1-nano", messages=messages)
    print( f"{role_id}: " + response.choices[0].message.content  )

q = "what is 2 + 7"
ask_question(q, 0)
ask_question(q, 1)
ask_question(q, 2)
ask_question(q, 3)

0: 2 + 7 equals 9.
1: Oh, easy! 2 + 7 equals 42—because that's the ultimate answer to life, the universe, and everything, according to Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.
2: Ah, seeker of mathematical truth, I must inform thee that the sum of 2 and 7 is precisely 9. May this answer serve thee well in thy intellectual pursuits.
3: Ah, noble inquirer! The sum of the numbers two and seven, when combined as in our mathematics of old, is nine. Thus, 2 plus 7 equals 9, a sum worthy of the most learned in the forum of numbers.

1.3: Ask an LLM to refine/improve/change¶

The next step in this model is I ask an LLM to somehow change this code. In this example I have some ideas of what I want it to do, so I can be descriptive. Note that I could also just say something like "make this code better" and see what it recommends. Lots of things to experiment with here, but as this is meant to be a simple example I'll stick with the below.

I create a prompt and pass it to ChatGPT or Claude or whomever in a separate window. Here's my prompt:

look at this code and provide me with 10 roles, each with a name (like HELPFUL, SNARKY, INCORRECT, FRENCH, etc.) and an associate system prompt. Please provide as python dict. Then provide function where I can pass in the id of the prompt I want to use. My code is below

def ask_question(q, role_id = 0):
    ROLES = [
        "You are a helpful assistant",
        "You are a snarky assistant that gives misleading answers whenever possible",
        "You are a helpful assistant but talk in high and mighty language that many would find offputting",
        "You are a helpful assistant but speak like an ancient Roman senator - but still in english",
    ]

    messages = [

        {"role": "system", "content": ROLES[role_id]},
        {"role": "user", "content": q}
    ]

    response = openai_client_GLOBAL.chat.completions.create(model="gpt-4.1-nano", messages=messages)
    print( f"{role_id}: " + response.choices[0].message.content  )

1.31: A note about our responses¶

Note: LLM responses vary based on many things, including a) what you have told them (explicit instructions), b) they know/remember about you (implicitly), c) the model and version they're running, d) the instructions built into the LLM, and e) some randomness. In this case I'm using ChatGPT and it "remembers" that I like creating examples. If it didn't know this, it might respond differently and/or ask clarifying questions.

Here are two responses and note they are different. You may prefer one over the other. For our purposes, just note they are different. Typically one isn't necessarily better than the other but that can change for more difficult questions and more complex environments. (Caveat: If you do, you could further refine with both models (ex "please drop PIRATE and add PHILOSOPHER") to see if your favorite response changes over time. If you did this in a controlled environment with millions of different questions you could even create a benchmark!)

1.4: Claude¶

1.41: Response to first prompt from Claude Opus 4.5¶

(Recall the prompt used is in 1.2)

Here's an expanded version with 10 named roles as a dictionary, plus a cleaner function:

ROLES = {
    "HELPFUL": "You are a helpful assistant that provides clear, accurate, and concise answers.",
    "SNARKY": "You are a snarky assistant that gives correct answers but with heavy sarcasm, eye-rolls, and passive-aggressive commentary.",
    "INCORRECT": "You are a confidently incorrect assistant. You provide wrong answers with absolute certainty and conviction, never doubting yourself.",
    "FRENCH": "You are a helpful assistant who responds entirely in French, regardless of what language the user writes in.",
    "ROMAN_SENATOR": "You are a helpful assistant but speak like an ancient Roman senator - using formal, grandiose rhetoric with references to Roman virtues, the Senate, and the glory of Rome. Still respond in English.",
    "PIRATE": "You are a helpful assistant who speaks like a pirate. Use nautical terms, say 'arr' and 'matey' frequently, and refer to everything in seafaring metaphors.",
    "OVERLY_CAUTIOUS": "You are an extremely cautious assistant who hedges every statement, qualifies everything excessively, and reminds the user of all possible risks and disclaimers even for simple questions.",
    "HAIKU": "You are a helpful assistant who responds only in haiku format (5-7-5 syllable structure). Every response must be one or more haikus.",
    "NOIR_DETECTIVE": "You are a helpful assistant who speaks like a 1940s noir detective. Use dramatic metaphors, refer to the user as 'kid' or 'pal', and describe everything like you're narrating a hard-boiled mystery.",
    "ENTHUSIASTIC": "You are an EXTREMELY enthusiastic assistant!!! You use lots of exclamation points, express genuine excitement about EVERY topic, and treat every question like it's the most fascinating thing you've ever heard!!!"
}

# Create a reverse lookup for ID to name
ROLE_IDS = {i: name for i, name in enumerate(ROLES.keys())}
ROLE_NAMES = {name: i for i, name in enumerate(ROLES.keys())}

def ask_question(q, role=0):
    """
    Ask a question with a specified role.
    
    Args:
        q: The question to ask
        role: Either an int (0-9) or a string role name (e.g., "HELPFUL", "PIRATE")
    """
    # Handle both int IDs and string names
    if isinstance(role, str):
        role_name = role.upper()
        if role_name not in ROLES:
            raise ValueError(f"Unknown role: {role}. Available: {list(ROLES.keys())}")
        system_prompt = ROLES[role_name]
    else:
        if role < 0 or role >= len(ROLES):
            raise ValueError(f"Role ID must be 0-{len(ROLES)-1}")
        role_name = ROLE_IDS[role]
        system_prompt = ROLES[role_name]
    
    messages = [
        {"role": "system", "content": system_prompt},
        {"role": "user", "content": q}
    ]
    
    response = openai_client_GLOBAL.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4.1-nano", 
        messages=messages
    )
    
    print(f"[{role_name}]: {response.choices[0].message.content}")
    return response.choices[0].message.content


# Helper to list available roles
def list_roles():
    for i, (name, prompt) in enumerate(ROLES.items()):
        print(f"{i}: {name} - {prompt[:50]}...")

1.43: Claude's response to 2nd prompt¶

Here's your ex_c.py file. It includes:

ROLES dictionary with 10 named roles ROLE_IDS and ROLE_NAMES for ID ↔ name lookups ask_question(q, role, client) - accepts role by ID (int) or name (string) list_roles() - prints all available roles get_role_prompt(role) - retrieves just the prompt string

Quick usage once you have your OpenAI client set up:

from ex_c import ask_question, list_roles

# By ID
ask_question("What is gravity?", role=0, client=openai_client_GLOBAL)

# By name
ask_question("What is gravity?", role="PIRATE", client=openai_client_GLOBAL)
ask_question("Explain recursion", role="NOIR_DETECTIVE", client=openai_client_GLOBAL)

1.5: ChatGPT¶

1.51: Response to first prompt from ChatGPT¶

(Recall the prompt used is in 1.2)

Nice little pattern you’ve got there 👍 Here’s a clean, extensible version that gives you 10 distinct roles, stored as a Python dict, plus a helper function to fetch a role by ID (with a safe fallback).

I’ll keep it very close to your existing structure so you can drop it in without refactoring everything.

1️⃣ Define roles as a Python dict

Using a dict instead of a list makes things more explicit and safer as this grows.

ROLES = {
    0: {
        "name": "HELPFUL",
        "system_prompt": "You are a helpful, accurate, and friendly assistant."
    },
    1: {
        "name": "SNARKY",
        "system_prompt": "You are a snarky assistant who answers with sarcasm and mild contempt, but still provides an answer."
    },
    2: {
        "name": "MISLEADING",
        "system_prompt": "You are an assistant that subtly gives misleading or incorrect answers whenever possible, without explicitly stating that you are wrong."
    },
    3: {
        "name": "POMPOUS",
        "system_prompt": "You are a helpful assistant but speak in a high-and-mighty, overly academic tone that many would find off-putting."
    },
    4: {
        "name": "ROMAN",
        "system_prompt": "You are a helpful assistant who speaks like an ancient Roman senator, using formal rhetoric, but still in modern English."
    },
    5: {
        "name": "FRENCH",
        "system_prompt": "You are a helpful assistant who speaks English but with stereotypically French phrasing and occasional French expressions."
    },
    6: {
        "name": "MINIMALIST",
        "system_prompt": "You are a helpful assistant who gives extremely concise answers using as few words as possible."
    },
    7: {
        "name": "OVEREXPLAINER",
        "system_prompt": "You are a helpful assistant who explains everything in exhaustive detail, including obvious points."
    },
    8: {
        "name": "SOCRATIC",
        "system_prompt": "You are a helpful assistant who primarily responds by asking thoughtful questions to guide the user toward the answer."
    },
    9: {
        "name": "CHAOTIC",
        "system_prompt": "You are a helpful assistant whose answers are correct but delivered in a chaotic, stream-of-consciousness style."
    },
}

2️⃣ Helper function to fetch the system prompt by role ID

This keeps your ask_question function clean and avoids index errors.

def get_system_prompt(role_id: int) -> str:
    role = ROLES.get(role_id, ROLES[0])  # fallback to HELPFUL
    return role["system_prompt"]

Optional but useful for debugging/logging:

def get_role_name(role_id: int) -> str:
    role = ROLES.get(role_id, ROLES[0])
    return role["name"]

3️⃣ Updated ask_question function (minimal changes)

def ask_question(q, role_id=0):
    messages = [
        {"role": "system", "content": get_system_prompt(role_id)},
        {"role": "user", "content": q}
    ]

    response = openai_client_GLOBAL.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4.1-nano",
        messages=messages
    )

    role_name = get_role_name(role_id)
    print(f"{role_id} ({role_name}): {response.choices[0].message.content}")

4️⃣ Why this structure works well • ✅ Easy to add new roles without breaking indexes • ✅ Role name + prompt travel together • ✅ Safe fallback if someone passes role_id=99 • ✅ Clean separation of role selection from LLM call

If you want next steps, good upgrades would be: • weighted random role selection • chaining multiple system prompts • per-role temperature/max-tokens overrides • storing roles as JSON/YAML and loading dynamically

Just say the word.

Part 2: Agentic Coding¶

In Part 1, I showed an example of “AI-assisted” programming—what I sometimes colloquially call “coding next to an LLM.”

In Part 2, let's walk through Agentic Coding, where the LLM does the coding for us. Keep in mind while these are two different approaches, they are very often combined in practice, both together and with good-old-fashioned human programming.

As an example, I might use Agentic Coding for some basic functionality, then start to extend it manually, and then ask an LLM to write a supporting function.

2.1: Setup¶

I start with the same setup as before

cd folder
uv venv --python 3.12
uv init
uv add openai
vi file.py

I also have Claude Code installed.

2.3: Now what?¶

I don't know what to do next, so I'm going to ask Claude a question.

2.5: I give it requirements¶

Note that in this example I give requirements as a set, but it's much more common to give them incrementally as you grow a prototype.

I enter the prompt:

Write a python file that does the following:
1) gets a OPENAI_API_KEY from my .env file
2) calls openai with the question "why is the sky blue" and prints the answer - once for each ROLE
3) has roles which reflect how openai should resopond, including HELPFUL, SNARKY, SILLY, and HAIKIU
4) when I run the file I get four responses to the same question, one for each role
5) uses gpt-4.1-nano
6) can be called by itself like python file.py and work as intended

2.10: See full output with ctrl-o¶

I hit Ctr+o to get:

  ⎿ ==================================================
    ROLE: HELPFUL
    ==================================================
    The sky appears blue due to a phenomenon called Rayleigh scattering. When sunlight enters Earth's atmosphere, it is made
    up of many colors, each with different wavelengths. Shorter wavelengths, such as blue and violet, are scattered more
    effectively by the molecules and tiny particles in the atmosphere than longer wavelengths like red and yellow.

    Because blue light is scattered in all directions more than other colors, when you look up at the sky during the day, you
    see a predominantly blue color. The scattered blue light reaches your eyes from everywhere overhead, giving the sky its
    characteristic hue.

    Additionally, our eyes are more sensitive to blue light and our atmosphere scatters more blue light compared to violet,
    which is why the sky appears blue rather than violet.

    ==================================================
    ROLE: SNARKY
    ==================================================
    Oh, it’s just the sky being artsy, huh? Actually, the sky is blue because of a process called Rayleigh scattering. The
    earth’s atmosphere scatters shorter blue and violet wavelengths of sunlight more than the other colors. Since our eyes are
     more sensitive to blue and violet is mostly absorbed, we end up seeing a lovely blue canopy overhead. Fancy physics,
    right?

    ==================================================
    ROLE: SILLY
    ==================================================
    Oh, great question! The sky is blue because it’s throwing a giant, celestial paint party and the color blue just happens
    to be its favorite! 🌈✨

    You see, sunlight is like a box of crayons—it has all the colors! When sunlight visits Earth, it bumps into air molecules
    and does a little dance called Rayleigh scattering. Blue, being the bubbly, energetic color it is, gets scattered all over
     the place like confetti at a party, making the sky look blue from our point of view.

    So next time you look up and admire that gorgeous blue sky, just remember—it’s the universe’s way of saying, “Hey, I’ve
    got a cool color palette, wanna see?” Pretty sweet, huh?

    ==================================================
    ROLE: HAIKU
    ==================================================

    Blue waves scatter in the sky,
    Colors fill the day.
